title: Imperfect Symmetry: A Humanistic-Relational Model of Negotiated Power and Dignity in Psychotherapy
abstract: Some humanistic, relational, and collaborative traditions describe psychotherapy through ideals of equality, collaboration, and mutual recognition, although therapeutic relationships remain structurally asymmetrical: one person seeks help while the other holds professional authority, interpretive influence, and responsibility for the frame. This conceptual article proposes Imperfect Symmetry as a humanistic-relational model for distinguishing oppressive or humiliating asymmetries from those that can become clinically useful, dignity-preserving, and repairable. The model asks when asymmetries become sufficiently just, explicit, and negotiable to support growth. Drawing on attachment, humanistic-existential, systemic, cognitive, recognition-theoretical, common-factors, critical, and multicultural traditions, the article defines dignity as equal moral worth and relational authorship under unequal conditions. It articulates three levels of asymmetry—intrapsychic, interpersonal, and institutional—and a six-step clinical cycle: detect, locate, name, test, negotiate, and repair. The article also addresses the naturalization of power—the treatment of historically and culturally produced hierarchies as if they were natural or inevitable and outlines implications for alliance, consent, rupture–repair, supervision, and human science research.
